title: Statistics for Trading Research
tagline: Dependence, regression of a return on a signal, testing, regimes and resampling
summary: Trading rules are claims about dependence in returns. This course sets up expectation, variance and autocorrelation, the regression of a future return on a signal known today, hypothesis tests under multiple looks at the same history, stationarity and regimes, and resampling methods that respect time order.
overview: Probability and statistics are taught in full in the Maths Atlas. This course does not repeat that development. It specialises the pieces a trading experiment actually uses: the mean and variance of a return, the covariance that diversification relies on, and the autocorrelation that trend and mean-reversion stories are arguing about.

A signal is interesting only if it lines up with a later return. The regression chapter writes that sentence as a model, with the signal lagged so that the fit cannot see the future. Hypothesis tests then ask whether a slope or a mean excess return is distinguishable from noise — and, just as importantly, whether the test still means anything after many rules have been tried on the same years.

Returns are not a single stationary draw. Volatility clusters, correlations rise in stress, and a rule estimated in one regime can fail in the next. The last chapter replaces the fantasy of an i.i.d. sample with block bootstrap and related resamples that keep local dependence.
Nothing here is a claim that a particular pattern will persist. The course supplies the language in which later courses state their hypotheses and the tests those hypotheses have to survive.
outcomes: Compute the mean, variance, covariance and autocorrelation of a return series and interpret each one.
Fit a regression of a next-period return on a signal known at the decision time, and read the slope, residual and R-squared.
State a hypothesis test for a mean excess return and explain why many trials on one history inflate false discoveries.
Distinguish a stationary return model from a price level, and describe a simple two-regime picture of volatility.
Resample a dependent return series with a block bootstrap and say what the resulting interval does and does not cover.
Point to the matching theorem in the Maths Atlas when a proof belongs there rather than here.

chapters.title: Moments and dependence
chapters.summary: Expectation, variance, covariance and autocorrelation of returns, and what each one is evidence for.

chapters.title: Regression of a return on a signal
chapters.summary: A lagged signal as a regressor, least squares, and why a same-bar regression is not a forecast.

chapters.title: Tests and data snooping
chapters.summary: Tests of a mean or a slope, and the multiplicity problem when many rules see one history.

chapters.title: Stationarity and regimes
chapters.summary: Why price levels are not stationary, volatility clustering, and a two-state picture of calm and stress.

chapters.title: Resampling a return series
chapters.summary: The i.i.d. bootstrap, the block bootstrap, and intervals for a mean or a Sharpe ratio.

history.title: Théorie de la spéculation
history.detail: Bachelier modelled the price of a French government bond as a random walk and derived an option formula. The dissertation is the start of the mathematical theory of speculative prices.

history.title: Efficient capital markets
history.detail: Fama’s review organised the evidence on whether prices reflect information, and gave the weak, semi-strong and strong forms that later empirical work argues with.

history.title: Prices do not follow random walks
history.detail: Lo and MacKinlay rejected the random-walk hypothesis for weekly US stock returns using a variance-ratio test. Dependence can be statistically detectable and still economically small.

history.title: A reality check for data snooping
history.detail: White gave a bootstrap test of whether the best rule in a large search beats the benchmark, once the search itself is taken into account.

history.title: The cross-section of expected returns
history.detail: Harvey, Liu and Zhu documented the multiplicity behind the factor literature and argued that published t-statistics overstate the evidence.

references.title: The Econometrics of Financial Markets
references.authors: John Y. Campbell, Andrew W. Lo and A. Craig MacKinlay
references.note: The standard bridge from statistics to returns, predictability and event studies.

references.title: Analysis of Financial Time Series
references.note: Autocorrelation, volatility models and resampling, with worked financial series.

references.title: A Reality Check for Data Snooping
references.note: Econometrica. The paper to read before treating the winner of a search as a discovery.

references.title: … and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
references.authors: Campbell R. Harvey, Yan Liu and Heqing Zhu

references.title: All of Statistics
